cards.front: Match each biomolecule class to its building block.
cards.back: Carbohydrate = simple sugar (monosaccharide); Protein = amino acid; Nucleic acid = nucleotide; Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids

cards.front: Carbon can form {{4}} covalent bonds, so it builds long chains and rings.
cards.back: Carbon can form 4 covalent bonds, so it builds long chains and rings.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw one carbon atom in the middle with 4 bonds to H, then extend it into a short chain and a ring.

cards.front: Which elements make up proteins?
cards.back: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (some also have sulfur).

cards.front: Lipids do not mix with water because they are {{nonpolar}} (hydrophobic).
cards.back: Lipids do not mix with water because they are nonpolar (hydrophobic).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a triglyceride: one glycerol 'head' with three long wavy fatty-acid tails. Color the tails green.

cards.front: Name the hidden parts of this piece of DNA (a nucleic acid).
cards.back: sugar-phosphate backbone, base pair, hydrogen bonds, nucleotide

cards.front: Put the steps of making a working protein in order.
cards.back: Amino acids join by peptide bonds → A polypeptide chain forms → The chain folds into a 3D shape → A working protein
items: Amino acids join by peptide bonds
The chain folds into a 3D shape
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw beads on a string (amino acids), then show the string folding into a compact shape.

cards.front: What bond joins two amino acids, and what small molecule is released?
cards.back: A peptide bond; one water molecule is released (condensation).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two amino acids side by side, then joined, with a drop of water leaving.

cards.front: State the central dogma in one line.
cards.back: DNA → RNA → protein (transcription, then translation).

cards.front: Transcription makes {{mRNA}} from a DNA template in the {{nucleus}}.
cards.back: Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template in the nucleus.

cards.front: Order the journey from gene to protein in a eukaryote.
cards.back: Gene is transcribed to pre-mRNA → Introns are spliced out → Mature mRNA leaves the nucleus → Ribosome reads codons → Polypeptide is built

cards.front: Why is DNA replication called semi-conservative?
cards.back: Each new DNA molecule keeps one old strand and gets one new strand.

cards.front: Match each base to its partner.
cards.back: A in DNA = T; G = C; A in RNA = U
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a ladder of 4 base pairs. Color A-T green and G-C grey. Write the number of hydrogen bonds on each rung (2 and 3).

cards.front: What is a codon?
cards.back: Three mRNA bases that code for one amino acid (or a start/stop signal). Example: AUG = Met, start.

cards.front: RNA processing removes {{introns}}, joins {{exons}}, and adds a 5′ cap and poly-A tail.
cards.back: RNA processing removes introns, joins exons, and adds a 5′ cap and poly-A tail.

cards.front: Name each hidden label in this animal cell.
cards.back: lysosome, rough ER, mitochondrion, cell membrane, centriole, nucleus, Golgi apparatus

cards.front: Name each hidden label in this plant cell.
cards.back: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus, large vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondrion

cards.front: State the three ideas of the cell theory.
cards.back: 1) All living things are made of cells. 2) The cell is the basic unit of life. 3) New cells come only from existing cells.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three icons: a cluster of cells in a leaf, one cell labeled 'unit of life', and one cell dividing into two.

cards.front: Match each organelle to its job.
cards.back: Mitochondrion = makes ATP; Ribosome = builds proteins; Lysosome = digests waste; Golgi = packages and ships proteins; Chloroplast = photosynthesis

cards.front: Give two differences between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
cards.back: Prokaryotes: no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles, smaller. Eukaryotes: true nucleus and organelles.

cards.front: Total magnification = {{eyepiece}} × {{objective}} magnification.
cards.back: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective magnification.

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the light microscope.
cards.back: eyepiece, objective lens, stage, light source, focus knob, arm

cards.front: Match the organelle to its role.
cards.back: Peroxisome = breaks down hydrogen peroxide; Centriole = helps organize the spindle in animal cells; Cytoskeleton = protein fibers that give shape; Vacuole = stores water and solutes
pairs: helps organize the spindle in animal cells
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a cell. Add a peroxisome (small sphere), a pair of centrioles at right angles, fibers across the cytoplasm, and a vacuole.

cards.front: Put the stages of mitosis in order.
cards.back: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase

cards.front: What does mitosis produce?
cards.back: Two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent (diploid stays diploid).

cards.front: What does meiosis produce?
cards.back: Four genetically different haploid cells (half the chromosomes). Used to make gametes.

cards.front: Match the mitosis stage to what happens.
cards.back: Prophase = chromosomes condense; Metaphase = chromosomes line up at the equator; Anaphase = sister chromatids pulled apart; Telophase = two nuclei re-form
pairs: chromosomes line up at the equator

cards.front: Crossing over happens in {{prophase I}} of meiosis and creates new allele combinations.
cards.back: Crossing over happens in prophase I of meiosis and creates new allele combinations.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two homologous chromosome pairs touching, swapping a piece (one green, one grey), then separating.

cards.front: How many cell divisions are in mitosis and in meiosis?
cards.back: Mitosis: one division. Meiosis: two divisions (meiosis I and II) after one DNA copy.

cards.front: How many chromosomes are in a human body cell and in a human gamete?
cards.back: Body cell: 46 (2n). Gamete: 23 (n).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a body cell with '46' and an egg and a sperm each with '23'; show them joining to make 46.

cards.front: 6CO₂ + 6{{H₂O}} + light → {{C₆H₁₂O₆}} + 6O₂
cards.back: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

cards.front: Where does photosynthesis occur and what absorbs the light?
cards.back: In chloroplasts; chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a leaf, zoom into a cell, then into a chloroplast. Label chlorophyll in green.

cards.front: Name the main limiting factors of photosynthesis.
cards.back: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature (also water and chlorophyll).

cards.front: Order the steps of the starch test on a leaf.
cards.back: Keep plant in dark (destarch) → Expose leaf to light → Boil leaf in water → Warm leaf in ethanol → Rinse and add iodine

cards.front: Why is a leaf warmed in ethanol in the starch test?
cards.back: To remove the green chlorophyll so the blue-black iodine color can be seen. Heat the ethanol only in a hot-water bath.

cards.front: A variegated (green and white) leaf is tested for starch. Where is it blue-black?
cards.back: Only in the green parts: they have chlorophyll, so they photosynthesized and made starch.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a leaf with green and white patches, then the same leaf after iodine with only the green patches dark.

cards.front: Give two reasons photosynthesis is important.
cards.back: It makes food (glucose) for the food chain and releases oxygen while removing carbon dioxide.

cards.front: Aerobic respiration: glucose + {{oxygen}} → {{carbon dioxide}} + water + energy (about 30 ATP).
cards.back: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (about 30 ATP).

cards.front: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
cards.back: Ethanol and carbon dioxide, plus a little energy (fermentation).

cards.front: What is made in anaerobic respiration in muscle cells?
cards.back: Lactic acid and a little energy (about 2 ATP per glucose).

cards.front: Match each process to what it uses or makes.
cards.back: Photosynthesis = uses CO₂, makes O₂; Respiration = uses O₂, makes CO₂; Mitochondria = site of aerobic respiration; ATP = usable cell energy

cards.front: Is breathing the same as respiration?
cards.back: No. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the chemical release of energy inside cells.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw lungs on the left (breathing) and a cell with a mitochondrion on the right (respiration), linked by arrows for O₂ and CO₂.

cards.front: Plants carry out respiration in {{all}} living cells, {{day and night}}.
cards.back: Plants carry out respiration in all living cells, day and night.

cards.front: Why can muscles ache after a sprint?
cards.back: When oxygen is short, muscle cells make ATP anaerobically and lactic acid builds up.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a muscle cell with two paths from glucose: one with O₂ (lots of ATP) and one without (lactic acid, little ATP).

cards.front: Match each connective tissue to its job.
cards.back: Bone = supports and protects; Cartilage = flexible cushion; Ligament = bone to bone; Tendon = muscle to bone; Blood = transport

cards.front: What does epithelial tissue do and where is it?
cards.back: It forms a protective covering of the body surface and lines organs and cavities (skin, gut lining).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a row of tightly packed cells forming a sheet, with 'outside' above and 'inside' below.

cards.front: Describe skeletal muscle.
cards.back: Striated, voluntary, attached to bones by tendons, with many nuclei per fiber.

cards.front: Describe smooth muscle.
cards.back: Not striated, involuntary, one nucleus per cell. Found in the gut, blood vessels and bladder.

cards.front: Describe cardiac muscle.
cards.back: Striated, involuntary, branched cells joined by intercalated discs. Found only in the heart.

cards.front: Which tissue joins bone to bone, and which joins muscle to bone?
cards.back: Ligament: bone to bone. Tendon: muscle to bone.

cards.front: Why is blood a connective tissue?
cards.back: It has cells (red cells, white cells, platelets) in a fluid matrix (plasma) and links the body by transporting materials.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a test tube of blood that has separated into plasma on top, a thin white layer, and red cells at the bottom.

cards.front: Name each hidden organ.
cards.back: mouth, esophagus, liver, stomach, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine

cards.front: Order the path of food through the gut.
cards.back: Mouth → Esophagus → Stomach → Small intestine → Large intestine → Anus

cards.front: Match each gland to its secretion.
cards.back: Salivary glands = amylase; Gastric glands = HCl and pepsin; Liver = bile; Pancreas = pancreatic juice

cards.front: Where do most digestion and absorption happen, and why?
cards.back: In the small intestine: it is long and has villi, which give a huge surface area.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a close-up of one villus with a blood capillary and a lacteal inside it.

cards.front: Match the missing nutrient to the disease.
cards.back: Vitamin C = scurvy; Vitamin D = rickets; Iodine = goiter; Iron = anemia

cards.front: What does iodine solution test for, and what is a positive result?
cards.back: Starch: it turns from yellow-brown to blue-black.

cards.front: Name the classes of food in a balanced diet.
cards.back: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and fiber, in the right amounts.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a plate divided into sections for the seven food classes, with one food example in each.

cards.front: Is bile an enzyme? What does it do?
cards.back: No. Bile (made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fat into droplets so lipase can work faster.

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the respiratory system.
cards.back: trachea, bronchus, lung, alveoli, diaphragm

cards.front: Order the path of air to the alveoli.
cards.back: Nose → Trachea → Bronchus → Bronchiole → Alveoli

cards.front: What happens when you breathe in?
cards.back: Diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs move up and out, chest volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in.

cards.front: What happens when you breathe out?
cards.back: Diaphragm relaxes and domes up, ribs move down and in, chest volume falls, pressure rises, air is pushed out.

cards.front: How are alveoli built for gas exchange?
cards.back: Very thin walls, moist, huge total surface area and a dense network of capillaries; gases diffuse.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw one alveolus as a bubble wrapped in capillaries; arrows show O₂ in and CO₂ out.

cards.front: What is tissue respiration?
cards.back: Cells use oxygen to release energy from glucose in their mitochondria; heat is also produced.

cards.front: Breathing in: chest volume {{rises}}, pressure {{falls}}, so air moves in.
cards.back: Breathing in: chest volume rises, pressure falls, so air moves in.

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the urinary system.
cards.back: kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra

cards.front: Order the path of urine.
cards.back: Kidney → Ureter → Bladder → Urethra

cards.front: Match each organ to its excretory product.
cards.back: Kidneys = urea, water and salts (urine); Sweat glands = sweat; Lungs = carbon dioxide and water vapor
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a body outline with three arrows leaving: from the kidneys, from the skin and from the lungs. Label each product.

cards.front: What do the kidneys do with blood?
cards.back: Millions of nephrons filter the blood, remove urea and extra water and salts, and return the rest to the blood.

cards.front: Where is urea made?
cards.back: In the liver, from the breakdown of amino acids. The kidneys then remove it in urine.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw liver → blood → kidney → urine with 'urea' written along the arrows.

cards.front: Give two jobs of sweat.
cards.back: It cools the body by evaporating and removes water, salts and a little urea.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw skin with a sweat gland, a pore, and arrows showing sweat leaving and heat leaving.

cards.front: The kidney filters blood, the {{bladder}} stores urine, and the {{urethra}} carries it out.
cards.back: The kidney filters blood, the bladder stores urine, and the urethra carries it out.

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the brain and spinal cord.
cards.back: cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, spinal cord

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the reflex arc.
cards.back: receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the motor neuron.
cards.back: dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon terminals

cards.front: Order the reflex arc.
cards.back: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neuron → Spinal cord → Motor neuron → Effector → Response

cards.front: Match each brain part to its function.
cards.back: Cerebrum = thinking, memory, voluntary action; Cerebellum = balance and coordination; Medulla oblongata = heartbeat and breathing

cards.front: Match each nerve type to what it carries.
cards.back: Sensory nerve = impulses to the CNS; Motor nerve = impulses from the CNS to muscles or glands; Mixed nerve = both directions
pairs: impulses from the CNS to muscles or glands
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a spinal cord in the middle and three nerves: one arrow in, one arrow out, one with both arrows.

cards.front: What is a reflex action and why is it fast?
cards.back: An automatic, rapid response to a stimulus. The impulse goes through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain to decide.

cards.front: Compare innate and adaptive immunity.
cards.back: Innate: fast, general, no memory (skin, mucus, phagocytes). Adaptive: slower the first time, specific, has memory (B and T cells).

cards.front: Name each hidden part of this antibody drawing.
cards.back: antibody, binding site, antigen

cards.front: What do B cells do?
cards.back: When they meet their antigen they become plasma cells that make antibodies; some become memory cells.

cards.front: What do T cells do?
cards.back: Helper T cells coordinate the response; killer T cells destroy body cells infected by viruses.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a killer T cell touching a virus-infected cell, with an arrow labeled 'destroys'.

cards.front: Why is a second infection usually milder?
cards.back: Memory cells remember the antigen and make antibodies faster and in larger amounts.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a graph: antibody level vs time with a small first peak and a bigger, faster second peak.

cards.front: What is an allergy?
cards.back: An overreaction of the immune system to a harmless substance (allergen) such as pollen, dust mites or peanuts; symptoms: sneezing, itching, rash.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a pollen grain entering the nose and arrows to symptoms: sneezing, watery eyes, itching.

cards.front: Match each innate defense to how it works.
cards.back: Skin = physical barrier; Mucus and cilia = trap and sweep out germs; Stomach acid = kills germs; Phagocytes = engulf germs

cards.front: Name each hidden gland.
cards.back: pituitary gland, thyroid gland, pancreas, adrenal gland

cards.front: How do endocrine and exocrine glands differ?
cards.back: Endocrine glands have no ducts and release hormones into the blood. Exocrine glands release products through ducts (sweat, saliva).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two glands: one with a tube (duct) leading out, one with no duct and an arrow into a blood vessel.

cards.front: Match each gland to a hormone.
cards.back: Pituitary = growth hormone; Thyroid = thyroxine; Adrenal = adrenaline; Pancreas = insulin

cards.front: What is a hormone?
cards.back: A chemical messenger made by an endocrine gland and carried by the blood to target organs.

cards.front: What do insulin and glucagon do?
cards.back: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it. Both come from the pancreas.

cards.front: Why is the pituitary called the master gland?
cards.back: Its hormones control other endocrine glands (such as the thyroid) and growth.

cards.front: What does adrenaline do?
cards.back: Prepares the body for fight or flight: faster heart rate, more blood to muscles, more glucose.

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the heart.
cards.back: vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, aorta, pulmonary vein, left atrium, bicuspid valve, left ventricle, septum

cards.front: Order the path of blood through the heart and lungs.
cards.back: Vena cava → Right atrium → Right ventricle → Pulmonary artery → Lungs → Pulmonary vein → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Aorta

cards.front: Why is the left ventricle wall the thickest?
cards.back: It pumps blood to the whole body at high pressure; the right ventricle only pumps to the lungs.

cards.front: What is double circulation?
cards.back: Blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit: right side to lungs and back, then left side to body and back.

cards.front: Match the vessel to its feature.
cards.back: Artery = thick wall, high pressure; Vein = valves, returns blood to heart; Capillary = one cell thick, exchange

cards.front: Who is the universal donor and universal acceptor?
cards.back: Group O is the universal donor; group AB is the universal acceptor.

cards.front: Name three heart conditions in the syllabus.
cards.back: Palpitations (felt irregular beat), cardiac arrest (heart stops pumping), hypertension (high blood pressure).

cards.front: What is the lymphatic system?
cards.back: A network of vessels and nodes parallel to blood vessels; it returns tissue fluid to the blood and helps fight infection.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a blood capillary leaking fluid into tissue, a lymph vessel collecting it, and a lymph node on the way.

cards.front: What do heart valves do?
cards.back: They keep blood flowing one way. Tricuspid: right atrium to right ventricle. Bicuspid: left atrium to left ventricle.

cards.front: Give two biotic and two abiotic factors.
cards.back: Biotic: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria. Abiotic: sunlight, temperature, water, soil.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a pond. Circle living things in green and write abiotic factors (sun, water, temperature) in grey.

cards.front: Match each role to its job.
cards.back: Producer = makes food by photosynthesis; Consumer = eats other organisms; Decomposer = breaks down dead matter

cards.front: Order this food chain from producer to top consumer.
cards.back: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk

cards.front: In a food web, which way do the arrows point?
cards.back: From the food to the organism that eats it: the direction energy flows.

cards.front: What does a pyramid of numbers show?
cards.back: The number of organisms at each trophic level; usually wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.

cards.front: Match each relationship to its effect (A / B).
cards.back: Mutualism = + / +; Commensalism = + / 0; Parasitism = + / −, lives on or in the host; Predation = + / −, kills and eats the prey
pairs: + / −, lives on or in the host

cards.front: How much energy passes to the next trophic level?
cards.back: Roughly 10 percent. The rest is lost as heat or used for life processes.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four stacked boxes (producer to top consumer) with 100, 10, 1, 0.1 units of energy and heat arrows leaving each.

cards.front: Match each kingdom to an example.
cards.back: Monera = bacteria; Protista = Amoeba; Fungi = bread mould; Plantae = mango tree; Animalia = fish

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the Amoeba.
cards.back: pseudopod, nucleus, food vacuole, cell membrane, contractile vacuole

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the bread mould.
cards.back: sporangium, spores, sporangiophore, rhizoids, hyphae

cards.front: Name the three common bacterial shapes.
cards.back: Cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods) and spirilla (spirals).

cards.front: Name each hidden part of the bacterium.
cards.back: cell wall, nucleoid, plasmid, flagellum, ribosomes

cards.front: Why do scientists classify living things?
cards.back: To identify organisms, show how they are related, and make studying millions of species easier.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a kitchen cupboard sorted into groups (spices, tins, grains) and write one sentence: classification = sorting by shared features.

cards.front: How do fungi feed?
cards.back: Hyphae release enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the digested food (saprotrophic). Cell walls contain chitin.

cards.front: How does an Amoeba move, feed and reproduce?
cards.back: It moves and engulfs food with pseudopodia, and reproduces by binary fission.

cards.front: What separates vertebrates from invertebrates?
cards.back: Vertebrates have a backbone (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals); invertebrates do not (insects, worms).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a fish and an insect; add a line of vertebrae to the fish only.
